title: India's Medical Tourism Market Crosses $20 Billion as Patient Arrivals Triple Since 2020
excerpt: Driven by cost savings of up to 80%, expanding visa access and stronger safety standards, India is rapidly closing the gap with Thailand and Singapore as a global healthcare destination.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • India's medical tourism market is projected to grow from $20.4 billion in 2026 to $65.1 billion by 2036.
  • International patient arrivals surged from 1.83 lakh in 2020 to 6.59 lakh in 2023.
  • Complex procedures in India cost 60-80% less than in Western countries, e.g., heart bypass at $5,000.
  • Five new Regional Medical Hubs are proposed to enhance India's medical tourism infrastructure.
  • India's healthcare system includes over 69,000 hospitals and 1.2 million registered doctors.

  • India's medical tourism market is valued at $20.4 billion in 2026, projected to reach $65.1 billion by 2036 at a 12.3% CAGR, according to Future Market Insights.
  • International patient arrivals have more than tripled from 1.83 lakh in 2020 to 6.59 lakh in 2023, with the e-Medical Visa now covering 167 countries.
  • Complex procedures cost 60-80% less than in Western countries — heart bypass surgery starts at $5,000 in India versus $150,000 in the United States.
  • The Union Budget 2026-27 proposes five new Regional Medical Hubs to expand capacity and strengthen India's position against competitors like Thailand and Singapore.

India's medical tourism sector has entered a new phase. The market, valued at $20.4 billion in 2026 according to Future Market Insights, is projected to reach $65.1 billion by 2036 — expanding at a 12.3% compound annual growth rate. What was once a price-driven industry is evolving into an organized, safety-focused healthcare travel ecosystem.

The growth is visible in the numbers. Medical tourist arrivals climbed from 1.83 lakh in 2020 to 6.59 lakh in 2023, according to government data cited by NDTV. The figure held steady at 6.44 lakh in 2024, while provisional data for January through November 2025 had already crossed 4.5 lakh. Union Tourism Minister Gajendra Singh Shekhawat noted that India recorded 1,31,856 foreign tourist arrivals for medical purposes from January to April 2025 alone, accounting for about 4.1% of total inbound arrivals.

Cost Remains King, But the Game Has Changed

India's core advantage remains affordability. Heart bypass surgery starts at roughly $5,000 in India, compared with nearly $150,000 in the United States. Knee replacement costs $5,500 to $9,500 versus $30,000 to $70,000 in the US. IVF treatment ranges from $2,300 to $5,000, against $12,000 to $15,000 in many Western countries. Across the board, complex procedures cost 60% to 80% less, according to NDTV.

But industry leaders say cost alone no longer explains the growth. "The industry is no longer competing only on affordability. International patients now expect a complete healthcare experience, with safety, coordination and post-treatment support becoming equally important," said Sahil Jain, co-founder and CEO of The Medical Travel Company (TMTC).

Organized medical travel companies now bundle airport transfers, accommodation for attendants, physiotherapy, nutrition support and recovery services into comprehensive treatment packages. Some operators include 12-month post-surgery insurance for orthopaedic procedures and dental implants. For patients from African countries, coverage may extend to emergency medical evacuation.

Infrastructure and Accreditation Scale Up

India's healthcare infrastructure has expanded to support the surge. The country now has 69,364 hospitals — 43,486 private and 25,778 public — staffed by 1.2 million registered doctors, according to government data reported by Travel and Tour World. The National Accreditation Board for Hospitals and Healthcare Providers (NABH) has accredited more than 1,299 hospitals based on over 600 safety parameters. Several Indian institutions also hold Joint Commission International (JCI) accreditation.

The government's e-Medical Visa programme, which now covers citizens of 167 countries, has reduced friction for incoming patients. An AYUSH Visa category, introduced in July 2023, caters specifically to international visitors seeking traditional Indian therapies including Ayurveda, Yoga and Naturopathy.

"The focus has shifted from offering the cheapest treatment to ensuring the patient feels supported throughout the journey."

— Sahil Jain, Co-Founder and CEO, The Medical Travel Company

Closing the Gap With Regional Rivals

Despite its rapid growth, India still trails Thailand, Singapore and the UAE in delivering integrated patient experiences. Patients often have to coordinate separately with hospitals, hotels and transport providers, according to Jain. Countries like Thailand have built stronger reputations by offering seamless end-to-end services.

The Union Budget 2026-27 addresses this directly by proposing five Regional Medical Hubs across India through public-private partnerships. These hubs would combine specialized medical centres, AYUSH wellness facilities, diagnostic services and dedicated support desks for international patients under a single integrated model.

Major cities — Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, Bengaluru and Hyderabad — already serve as established medical tourism centres. Cardiovascular treatment leads demand with a 31.6% market share, while patients aged 36 to 55 account for 38.9% of medical tourism arrivals, according to Future Market Insights.

What This Means for the Diaspora

For NRIs and members of the Indian diaspora, the sector's maturation has practical implications. Many already travel to India for elective procedures — dental work, knee replacements, fertility treatments — drawn by the cost differential and familiarity with the system. The expansion of post-treatment support, including coordination with healthcare providers in patients' home countries, makes the proposition more viable for complex procedures that require long-term follow-up.

India's medical tourism industry may have been built on low costs, but its next chapter will be defined by trust, safety and patient experience. The infrastructure to support that transition is now being put in place.
